chunks: And from him, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Abu al-Khattab, from Wahb ibn Hafsh, from Abu Basir, who said:
I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): A man fasted a day of voluntary fast, then ate and drank forgetfully. He said: 'He completes that day, and there is nothing upon him.'

The Sheikh (may Allah have mercy on him) said: If he deliberately broke his fast before midday (zawal), there is nothing upon him, and he fasts one day in its place whenever he wishes. And if he broke his fast after midday, expiation (kaffarah) becomes obligatory upon him, which is feeding ten poor people, and he fasts one day in its place. If feeding is not possible for him, he fasts three days in place of feeding. This is indicated by what he narrated:

key_terms.الزَّوَالِ: Midday (when the sun begins to decline)
key_terms.بَدَلَهُ: In its place / instead of it

ai.seo_question: What is the difference in ruling for breaking a voluntary fast deliberately before or after midday in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* establishes the jurisprudential distinction between forgetful and deliberate breaking of voluntary fasts, highlighting the role of *al-zawal* (midday) as the critical threshold for expiation liability. It reflects the Shia scholarly tradition where deliberate breaking after midday incurs *kaffarah* (feeding ten poor or fasting three days), whereas breaking before midday requires only *qada* (making up the day), underscoring the principle of gradual obligation in voluntary acts of worship.
